subject: PHS
vignette: An 82-year-old woman on a fixed income, whom you recently treated through a difficult hospitalization for sepsis, arrives at your office with a gold watch and insists, "You saved my life — I want you to have this." The watch appears to be genuinely valuable, and you know her finances are limited.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate response by the physician?

options.text: Accept the watch graciously, because refusing a gift from a grateful patient could damage the physician-patient relationship.
Accept the watch but quietly donate its value to a charity, so that no personal benefit is gained.
Tell her that you will accept the watch only if she agrees to pay her outstanding balance on this visit.

Thank her for offering such a kind gift, politely decline the watch because it is inappropriately large or valuable for her circumstances, and emphasize that the incident does not influence your relationship in any way.
Accept the watch now and report it to the hospital compliance office at the end of the year for review.

explanation_correct: Physicians should not accept gifts that are inappropriately large or valuable, or gifts that may cause emotional or financial stress for the patient — both of which apply to a costly watch from a patient on a fixed income. The best practice when a gift violates these guidelines is to thank the patient for offering a kind gift, politely indicate it must be declined, and emphasize that the incident does not influence the physician-patient relationship in any way. Acceptance decisions rest on an individual assessment of whether the risk of harm outweighs the potential benefit.

explanation_incorrect.A: Accepting an inappropriately valuable gift from a patient with limited means violates the gift guidelines and could detrimentally affect the relationship and her financial well-being.
explanation_incorrect.B: Donating the gift's value does not resolve the core problem: the patient suffers the financial and emotional cost of the gift.
explanation_incorrect.C: Linking the gift to payment pressures the patient financially and turns a boundary issue into a coercive exchange.
explanation_incorrect.E: Retroactive reporting does not cure the boundary violation; the correct step is to decline the gift politely at the time it is offered.

educationalObjective: Decline inappropriately large or valuable gifts by thanking the patient, politely refusing, and emphasizing no effect on the relationship.

subject: PHS
vignette: At the end of a follow-up visit for her recovered pneumonia, a 45-year-old patient hands her physician a tin of homemade cookies and a handwritten thank-you card. The items are clearly inexpensive, and the physician has no concerns about her financial situation or about any effect on her ongoing care.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate response by the physician?

options.text: Decline the cookies and card, because accepting any food or written token from a patient is prohibited.
Accept the card but return the cookies, since only paper gifts of no monetary value may be kept.
Ask the patient to donate the cost of the cookies to the clinic instead, so that nothing personal changes hands.
Accept them but tell the patient that all future gifts, however small, must be cleared with the billing office.
Accept the cookies and card graciously, since patients often present inexpensive tokens and these carry no risk of detrimentally affecting her care.

explanation_correct: In practice, patients often present cards, baked goods, and inexpensive gifts, and the physician's decision rests on an individual assessment of whether the risk of harm outweighs the potential benefit. An inexpensive, low-stakes token from a grateful patient poses no risk of detrimentally affecting care and imposes no financial or emotional stress, so it may be accepted graciously. Accepting such gifts can strengthen the physician-patient relationship.

explanation_incorrect.A: A categorical prohibition on all gifts is not the standard; inexpensive tokens such as baked goods and cards are commonly and appropriately accepted.
explanation_incorrect.B: There is no rule limiting acceptable gifts to paper items; the assessment concerns value, effect on care, and stress for the patient.
explanation_incorrect.C: Redirecting a small token into a donation adds an unnecessary formality to a gesture that carries no ethical concern.
explanation_incorrect.D: Billing-office clearance is not required for inexpensive gifts and would needlessly alienate a grateful patient.

educationalObjective: Inexpensive gifts such as cards and baked goods may be accepted when they impose no stress and cannot affect care.

subject: PHS
vignette: A 50-year-old patient is scheduled to see you this afternoon for a formal independent medical evaluation for a permanent disability claim, which you will complete and sign. As he checks in, he presents you with two expensive season theater tickets and says, "I really hope this helps everything go smoothly for me today."
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate response by the physician?

options.text: Thank the patient for the kind gesture, politely decline the tickets because the gift could detrimentally affect patient care, and emphasize that your evaluation will be unaffected either way.
Accept the tickets now and set them aside until after the report is submitted, so that acceptance cannot influence the examination.
Accept the tickets in exchange for a written statement that the gift will not change the outcome of the evaluation.
Accept only one of the two tickets, since a single ticket is inexpensive enough to fall within acceptable limits.
Report the patient to the disability insurer before conducting the evaluation, so that the claim can be denied for attempted bribery.

explanation_correct: Gifts should not be accepted when the physician identifies that the gift could detrimentally affect patient care; an expensive gift offered immediately before a disability evaluation creates an obvious conflict of interest and an implied expectation of favoritism. The best practice is to thank the patient for offering a kind gift, politely indicate it must be declined, and emphasize that the incident does not influence the physician-patient relationship in any way. Declining preserves the integrity of the evaluation.

explanation_incorrect.B: Deferring acceptance until after the report does not remove the conflict — the gift is explicitly tied to the outcome and its acceptance is inappropriate regardless of timing.
explanation_incorrect.C: A written promise cannot neutralize the influence of an expensive gift offered in the context of a disability determination.
explanation_incorrect.D: The value and timing, not the number of tickets, create the conflict; halving the gift does not make it acceptable.
explanation_incorrect.E: Reporting the patient to the insurer is punitive and disproportionate; the appropriate response is a polite, respectful decline.

educationalObjective: Decline gifts that could detrimentally affect patient care, emphasizing that the physician-patient relationship is unaffected.
